[Section: Sincerity of intention for God, the Exalted]

His saying: "Whoever's intention is sincere in the truth, even against himself, God will suffice him for what lies between him and the people, and whoever adorns himself with what is not in him, God will disgrace him." This is the twin of the words of prophethood, and it is fitting that it came forth from the niche of the inspired transmitter. These two phrases are among the treasures of knowledge, and of the best use of them is that one benefits others and oneself benefits to the utmost. As for the first phrase, it is the source and root of goodness, and the second is the root and branch of evil. For when a servant's intention is sincere for God, the Exalted, and his aim, his concern and his deed are for His Face, the Glorified, God is with him, for He, the Glorified, is "with those who are mindful of Him and those who are doers of good" [al-Nahl: 128]. The head of piety and excellence is sincerity of intention for God in establishing the truth. God, the Glorified, cannot be overcome, so whoever has Him with him, who can overcome him or touch him with harm? If God is with the servant, whom will he fear? And if He is not with him, whom will he hope in, and whom will he trust? And who will help him after Him?

When the servant upholds the truth against others and against himself first, and his standing is by God and for God, nothing will stand against him. Even if the heavens, the earth and the mountains plotted against him, God would suffice him their burden and would make for him a relief and a way out. The servant is only brought down through his negligence and shortcoming in these three matters, or in two of them, or in one. Whoever's standing is in falsehood is not helped, and if he is helped with a passing help, he has no outcome; he is blameworthy and forsaken. And if he stands for the truth but does not stand in it for God, rather he stands seeking praise, thanks and reward from creation, or to reach a worldly aim, which is the first thing intended while standing for the truth is a means to it, then victory is not guaranteed to him. For God only guarantees victory to those who strive in His way and fight so that the Word of God is the highest, not to one whose standing is for himself and his desire, for he is neither among the righteous nor among the good-doers. And if he is helped, it is in proportion to the truth he has with him, for God helps only the truth. When dominion belongs to the people of falsehood, it is in proportion to the patience they have, and patience is always victorious. If its bearer is righteous, he has victory and the outcome; and if he is a falsifier, he has no outcome. When a servant stands for the truth for God but stands by his own self and strength, and does not stand by God, seeking His help, relying upon Him, entrusting himself to Him, free of power and might except through Him, then he will have forsakenness and weakness of victory in proportion to what he has stood with of that. The crux of the matter is that the stripping of the two tawhids (unity) in the command of God, nothing whatsoever stands against it, and its bearer is strengthened and victorious even if the hosts of enemies succeed one another against him.

Imam Ahmad said: Dawud related to us, Shu'bah informed us, from Waqid ibn Muhammad ibn Zayd, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from 'A'ishah, who said: "Whoever angers people in pleasing God, the Mighty and Majestic, God will suffice him against people; and whoever pleases people by displeasing God, God will leave him to people."

[Section: The station of sincerity]

Among the stations of "You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" [al-Fatihah: 5] is the station of sincerity (ikhlas).

God, the Exalted, said: "And they were not commanded except to worship God, sincere to Him in religion" [al-Bayyinah: 5].

And He said: "Indeed We have sent down to you the Book with the truth, so worship God, sincere to Him in religion. Surely, to God belongs pure religion" [al-Zumar: 2-3].

And He said to His Prophet ﷺ: "Say: God do I worship, sincere to Him in my religion. So worship what you will other than Him" [al-Zumar: 14-15].

And He said to him: "Say: Indeed my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds. He has no partner, and with that I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims" [al-An'am: 162-163]. And He said: "He who created death and life that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed" [al-Mulk: 2].

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "It is the most sincere of it and the most correct of it."

They said: "O Abu 'Ali, what is its most sincere and most correct?" He said: "Indeed, when a deed is sincere but not correct, it is not accepted; and when it is correct but not sincere, it is not accepted. Until it is both sincere and correct. The sincere is that it be for God, and the correct is that it be upon the Sunnah."

Then he recited His saying, the Exalted: "So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord" [al-Kahf: 110].

And He, the Exalted, said: "And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God while being a doer of good?" [al-Nisa': 125].

So the submission of the face is the sincerity of aim and deed for God, and excellence in it is following His Messenger ﷺ and his Sunnah.

And He, the Exalted, said: "And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust" [al-Furqan: 23]. These are the deeds that were not according to the Sunnah, or in which something other than the Face of God was intended.

The Prophet ﷺ said to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may God be pleased with him: "Indeed you will not be left behind and do a deed seeking thereby the Face of God, the Exalted, except that you will increase in it in goodness, rank and elevation."

In the Sahih, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said:

"Three things the heart of a Muslim does not harbor rancour over: sincerity of deed for God, sincere counsel to the rulers of affairs, and adherence to the community of the Muslims, for their call surrounds them from behind."

That is, no rancour remains in it, and it does not carry rancour along with these three. Rather they remove its rancour from it, purify it from it, and bring it out of it. For the heart harbors the greatest rancour over shirk, and likewise it harbors rancour over deceit, and over departing from the community of the Muslims through innovation and misguidance. So these three fill it with rancour and corruption. The remedy for this rancour and the extraction of its impurities is by stripping away for sincerity and sincere counsel, and following the Sunnah.

The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked about the man who fights for show, and fights out of bravery, and fights out of zeal: which of these is in the way of God? He said: "Whoever fights so that the Word of God is the highest, he is in the way of God."

And he informed about the first three by whom the Fire will be kindled: the reciter of the Qur'an, the warrior, and the one who gives his wealth in charity, who did these things so that it would be said: "So-and-so is a reciter, so-and-so is brave, so-and-so is a giver of charity," and their deeds were not sincere for God.

And in the authentic divine hadith, God, the Exalted, says: "I am the most independent of partners from shirk. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I leave him and his shirk." [Wording as in the commentary: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in regard to shirk. Whoever does a deed in which he associates someone other than Me, it belongs to the one he associated, and I am free of it."]

And in another report, He says to him on the Day of Resurrection: "Go and take your reward from the one for whom you did the deed; you have no reward with Us."

And in the Sahih, from him ﷺ: "Indeed God does not look at your bodies, nor at your forms, but He looks at your hearts." And He, the Exalted, said: "Their flesh does not reach God, nor their blood, but piety from you reaches Him" [al-Hajj: 37].

And in a narrated divine report: "Sincerity is one of My secrets, which I have deposited in the heart of whoever I love of My servants."

Their expressions about sincerity and truthfulness have varied, while the aim is one.

It has been said: it is singling out the Truth, the Glorified, in aim within obedience.

And it has been said: it is purifying the act from observing the created beings.

And it has been said: it is guarding against observing creation, even observing oneself. And truthfulness is purifying oneself from looking at the self. So the sincere person has no showing-off, and the truthful person has no self-admiration. Sincerity is not complete except with truthfulness, nor truthfulness except with sincerity, and neither is complete except with patience.

And it has been said: whoever witnesses his sincerity as sincere, his sincerity needs a sincerity. So the deficiency of every sincere person in his sincerity is in proportion to his seeing of his sincerity. When the sight of sincerity falls away from his self, he becomes sincere and purified.

And it has been said: sincerity is the evenness of the servant's deeds in the outward and the inward. Showing-off is that his outward is better than his inward. And truthfulness in sincerity is that his inward is more flourishing than his outward.

And it has been said: sincerity is forgetting the sight of creation through continuous looking at the Creator. Whoever adorns himself before people with what is not in him falls from the eye of God.

From the sayings of al-Fudayl: Abandoning a deed for the sake of people is showing-off, and doing a deed for the sake of people is shirk, and sincerity is that God protects you from both of them.

Al-Junayd said: Sincerity is a secret between God and the servant. No angel knows it so as to write it, nor a devil so as to corrupt it, nor a desire so as to incline it.

It was said to Sahl: "What is hardest on the self?" He said: "Sincerity, because the self has no share in it."

Some of them said: Sincerity is that you do not seek a witness to your deed other than God, nor a rewarder other than Him.

Makhul said: No servant has ever been sincere for forty days except that the springs of wisdom appeared from his heart upon his tongue.

Yusuf ibn al-Husayn said: The most precious thing in this world is sincerity, and how much I strive to remove showing-off from my heart, yet it seems to sprout in another colour.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: When a servant becomes sincere, the abundance of whisperings and showing-off is cut off from him.

[Section: The degrees of sincerity]

[The first degree: removing the sight of the deed from the deed, and being freed from seeking a return for the deed]

Section

The author of "al-Manazil" said:

Sincerity: purifying the deed from every admixture.

That is, the deed is not mixed with impurities that come from the desires of the self, whether seeking adornment in the hearts of creation, or seeking their praise and fleeing their blame, or seeking their exaltation, or seeking their wealth, service, love, or fulfilment of his needs, or other causes and admixtures, whose collective bond is the will for other than God through one's deed, whatever it may be.

He said: It has three degrees. The first degree: removing the sight of the deed from the deed, being freed from seeking a return for the deed, and descending from contentment with the deed.

Three afflictions befall the doer in his deed: his seeing and observing it, seeking a return for it, and his contentment with it and resting upon it.

In this degree, he is freed from this trial. What frees him from seeing his deed is his witnessing God's favour upon him, His bounty, and His enabling him, and that he is by God and not by himself, and that it is the will of God that brought his deed into being, not his own will, as He, the Exalted, said: "And you do not will except that God wills, Lord of the worlds" [al-Takwir: 29].

Here it benefits him to witness compulsion (jabr), that he is a mere instrument, that his act is like the movements of trees and the blowing of winds, that the mover of it is other than him, the agent in it is other than him, that he is dead, and the dead does nothing, and that if he were left to himself, no good deed would come from him whatsoever. For the self is ignorant and wrongdoing, its nature is laziness and preference for appetites and idleness. It is the source of every evil and the abode of every ill. What is like this does not produce good, nor is that its nature.

So the good that comes from it is only from God and by Him, not from the servant and not by him, as He, the Exalted, said: "Were it not for the favour of God upon you and His mercy, not one of you would ever have been purified, but God purifies whom He wills" [al-Nur: 21]. And the people of Paradise said: "Praise be to God who guided us to this" [al-A'raf: 43]. And the Blessed and Exalted said to His Messenger ﷺ: "And had We not made you firm, you would have almost inclined toward them a little" [al-Isra': 74].

And He, the Exalted, said: "But God has made faith beloved to you and has made it beautiful in your hearts" [al-Hujurat: 7], and so on.

So every good in the servant is purely the bounty of God, His favour, His kindness and His blessing, and He is the one praised for it. Thus the servant's seeing of his deeds, in reality, is like his seeing of his created attributes: his hearing, his sight, his perception, his strength, indeed his health, the soundness of his limbs, and the like. All of it is purely the gift of God, His blessing, and His favour.

What frees the servant from this affliction is knowledge of his Lord and knowledge of his own self.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 98, verse 5 (part 2 of 2):

What frees a person from seeking a recompense for his deed is his knowledge that he is a pure slave ('abd mahd). A slave does not deserve a wage or a reward for serving his master, since he serves him by the requirement of his servitude ('ubudiyyah). Whatever he receives from his master of reward and recompense is then a bounty from Him, a kindness to him, and a favour upon him, not an exchange. A wage is due only to a free person or to the slave of another. As for a person's slave of his own, it is not due.

What frees a person from being pleased with his deed and from resting in it is two matters:

The first: observing its defects and faults, his shortcomings in it, the share of the self (hazz al-nafs) it contains, and the portion of Satan (nasib al-shaytan). Few are the deeds in which Satan has no portion, however small, and the self has a share in them.

The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about a man turning his head during prayer, and he said: "It is a snatching (ikhtilas) which Satan snatches from the prayer of the servant."

If this is the turning of the glance or the eye, then how is the turning of the heart toward other than Allah? This is the greatest portion of Satan from worship.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "Let none of you give Satan a share of his prayer, thinking it is a duty upon him not to turn away except to his right." He made this small, trifling amount a share and portion of Satan in the servant's prayer. So what is the assumption about what exceeds it?

As for the share of the self in the deed, none recognises it except the people of insight who are truthful.

The second: his knowledge of what the Lord, majestic is His majesty, deserves of the rights of servitude, its outward and inward manners, and its conditions, and that the servant is weaker, more incapable, and less than being able to fulfil it as a right, or to be content with it for his Lord. The one who knows (al-'arif) is not content with any of his deeds for his Lord, nor does he consider himself fit for Allah even for the blink of an eye. He feels shame at confronting Allah with his deed.

So his bad opinion of himself and his deed, his hatred of it, and his aversion to his breaths and their ascent to Allah prevent him from being content with his deed and from being content with himself.

Some of the early generations (salaf) used to pray four hundred rak'ahs in a day and night, then he would seize his beard and shake it, saying to himself: "O refuge of every evil! Have I been pleased with you for Allah even for the blink of an eye?"

One of them said: "The affliction of the servant is his contentment with himself. Whoever looks at himself with admiration for something in himself has destroyed himself. Whoever does not accuse himself at all times is deluded."

[Section: The second rank, shame from the deed together with exerting effort]

Section
The author of "al-Manazil" (Manazil al-Sa'irin, by al-Harawi al-Ansari) said:

"The second rank: shame (khajal) from the deed together with exerting one's utmost effort, and preserving one's striving by taking refuge from witnessing (the deed as one's own), and seeing the deed in the light of success (tawfiq) from the source of bounty (jud)."

These are three matters of his "shame" from his deed, which is the intensity of his modesty before Allah, since he does not see that deed as worthy of him, despite exerting his utmost effort in it. The Exalted said: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60].

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He is the man who fasts, prays, gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him."

One of them said: "I pray two rak'ahs and I rise from them like a thief or an adulterer whom people see, out of shame before Allah, mighty and majestic."

So the believer combines good deeds with fear and a bad opinion of himself. The deluded person has a good opinion of himself while he is doing wrong.

The second: preserving one's effort by taking refuge from witnessing, that is, he brings the utmost of his capacity in correcting the deed, shielding himself from witnessing it as coming from himself and by himself.

The third: that you take refuge in the light of success by which Allah illumines the insight of the servant. So, in the light of that illumination, you see that your deed comes from the source of His bounty, not by you and not from you.

This rank thus includes five things: a deed, striving in it, shame, modesty before Allah mighty and majestic, safeguarding oneself from witnessing it as from oneself, and seeing it as from the source of the bounty of Allah, glorified is He, and from Him.

[The third rank: sincerity of the deed by freedom from the deed]

He said: "The third rank: the sincerity of the deed through freedom from the deed. You leave it to move in the course of knowledge (sayr al-'ilm), and you move while witnessing the ruling, free from the bondage of the outward form (riqq al-rasm)."

The Shaykh explained his meaning of the sincerity of the deed from the deed by his words: "You leave it to move in the course of knowledge, and you move while witnessing the ruling."

The meaning of his words is: you make your deed follow knowledge, conforming to it and following it as a model. You move with its movement and stop with its stopping, and you move with its motion, descending to its stations, drinking from its sources, looking at the religious, commanding ruling, bound by it in doing and abstaining, seeking and fleeing. You look at the consequence of reward and punishment upon it as a cause and an acquisition. Along with that, you move with your heart, witnessing the cosmic, decreeing ruling in which causes and effects, movements and rests, are contained. Nothing remains there except pure will and the Lord's sole singularity in actions, and their source from His will and His purpose. So you are standing by the command and prohibition in doing and abstaining, moving by His movement, and by destiny and decree, in faith, witnessing, and truth. So you look at the Reality (haqiqah) and stand by the Law (shari'ah).

These two matters are the servitude of these two verses: ﴿For whoever among you wills to go straight, and you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Takwir: 28-29], and the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way. And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan: 29-30].

So leaving the deed to move in the course of knowledge: the station of ﴿For whoever among you wills to go straight﴾ [al-Takwir: 28], and his companion's movement while witnessing the ruling: the station of ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Takwir: 29].

As for his words "free from the bondage of the outward form": the freedom they refer to is not entering under the servitude of creation and the self, and entering under the bondage of servitude to the Truth alone.

By "the outward form" (rasm) they mean everything other than Allah, for all of it is outward forms (rusum). The rusum are traces (athar). The traces of abodes and dwellings are the marks that remain after their inhabitants. All created things, in the station of Reality, are traces and marks of the Power (al-qudrah). That is, you free your self from servitude to everything other than Allah, and you are with your heart with the Powerful, the Truth alone, not with the traces of His power, which are outward forms. So do not occupy yourself with other than Him, lest you occupy it with His servitude. Do not seek through your servitude to Him a state, a station, an unveiling (mukashafah), or anything other than Him.

These are four matters: exerting effort, adopting knowledge as judge, looking at the Reality, and freeing oneself from turning to other than Him. Allah is the Granter of success and the Helper.

[Section: The reality of sincerity is the unification of the sought]

Section
Sincerity is the non-division of the sought. Truthfulness (sidq) is the non-division of the seeking.

So the reality of sincerity is the unification of the sought, and the reality of truthfulness is the unification of seeking and will. Neither bears fruit except through pure submission to following (mutaba'ah).

These three pillars are the pillars of the journey and the foundations of the path. Whoever does not build his conduct and journey upon them is cut off. Even if he thinks he is travelling, his journey is either in the opposite direction to his goal, or it is the journey of a paralysed or shackled person, or the journey of the rider of a runaway mount, which, every time it takes a step forward, retreats ten steps backward.

If sincerity and following are absent, his journey is reversed backward. If he does not exert his utmost and does not unify his seeking, he travels like one who is shackled.

If all three are combined for him, then this is the one who cannot be matched on the course of his journey. That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills. And Allah is the Possessor of Great Bounty.

The believing, righteous servant is among the best of creation, so how can his testimony be rejected? Allah and His Messenger have declared him upright (ʿadl), as in the well-known hadith traced to the Prophet:

"The upright among every generation will carry this knowledge. They will remove from it the distortion of the extremists, the false attribution of the falsifiers, and the misinterpretation of the ignorant."

The servant who carries knowledge is upright by the explicit text of the Book and the Sunnah.

The scholars have also agreed that his report is accepted when he narrates a hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). How, then, can his testimony be accepted regarding the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while his testimony regarding one of the people is not accepted?

As for being pleased with Him (al-ridā ʿanhu, "His being pleased with them"), it is the servant's contentment with what He does to him and gives him. For this reason it occurs only in connection with reward and recompense, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ [al-Fajr: 27].

This, then, is her being pleased with Him because of the honour she has received from Him. Such is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will abide therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is for whoever fears his Lord﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 8].

Being pleased with Him (al-ridā bihi) is the root of being pleased with Him in the sense of His being pleased with you (al-ridā ʿanhu), and His being pleased with you is the fruit of your being pleased with Him.

The essence of the matter: being pleased with Him is tied to His names and attributes, while His being pleased with you is tied to His reward and recompense.

Also, the Prophet ﷺ linked tasting the sweetness of faith (dhawq ṭaʿm al-īmān) to whoever is pleased with Allah as Lord, and did not link it to whoever is pleased with Him (in the sense of being favoured by Him), as he ﷺ said: "Whoever is pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad ﷺ as Messenger, has tasted the sweetness of faith." He thus made being pleased with Him accompany being pleased with His religion and His Prophet. These three are the foundations of Islam, upon which it neither stands nor is established except by them and upon them.
